summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands and applies its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, as the instrument carrying its anti-discrimination provisions. Decisions of its Appeals Court in sexual-orientation cases have been reviewed by the Supreme Court of the Netherlands, which on 12 July 2024 upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Aruba for both male and female forms. The age of consent is 16 and is equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.

Article 1:221 of the Criminal Code defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed anywhere in the provision.

Parliament passed the civil-law amendment granting civil partnerships to same-sex couples on 8 September 2016 by 11 votes to 5, an Associated Press report of 9 September 2016 recording the same margin with four abstentions. The amendment extended civil-code marriage articles to registered same-sex unions and conferred spousal pension rights and emergency medical decision rights. Marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised kingdom-wide, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route. Same-sex marriage itself was established by the 12 July 2024 Supreme Court ruling.

Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge of 2004 to 2007, which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognise same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge. The Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition.

Several gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly.
tangentialFactors:
The official Aruba tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling safe, secure and welcome as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketer rather than independent evidence, but it documents how the island is positioned in mainstream tourism.

GlobalGayz describes Aruba as tolerant and mostly open, with a smaller and quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curaçao, and identifies Catholic influence as the main brake on further progress. It also records that the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands, and states that same-sex adoption is legal.

Regional positioning at the time of the 2016 vote: neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed same-sex unions, and Aruba was reported as the first island in the Caribbean to pass such a law.
localsOnly:
The registered-partnership campaign ran for two and a half years before the September 2016 vote. The openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes publicly introduced the bill in August 2016 as its sponsor, and an Igualdad Aruba petition gathered close to 20,000 signatures.

Numerous LGBT associations operate on the island, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and the Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. The last is quoted as saying that Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it is not in their face, that people are out but discreetly out, and that there has never been anything official.

Same-sex adoption is legal under Aruban law.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses gender markers or identity-document rules, entry and visa requirements, border screening, healthcare access, hate-crime sentence enhancement, or facility and restroom rules. Whether any other Aruban or Kingdom-level instrument covers gender identity and gender expression is unresolved, since the Criminal Code grounds cover sexual orientation only.

The age of consent of 16 is the only youth-specific legal threshold supplied by the sources; findings on schools, education, or minors' access to services and documentation are not sourced here.

The 2016 vote is reported as 11 to 5 in one account and as 11 to 5 with four abstentions in another; the discrepancy is unresolved.

The tourism board's safety claims are the destination's own marketing copy and are not independent verification of conditions on the ground.
